claims.text: The onset of melting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is governed by preferential diffusion and surface segregation of specific elements.
Surface segregation creates a transient surface-melted layer below the nominal bulk melting point.
The surface-melted layer propagates inward and accelerates the overall phase transition.
The starting nanoparticles are intended to be monodisperse, solid, single-phase, compositionally uniform, and minimally oxidized.
Localized surface compositional fluctuations reduce the local melting temperature.
The reduced local melting temperature initiates a thin surface liquid-like region that extends inward as temperature rises.
Interfacial-energy effects and element-specific segregation lower the melting threshold near the particle surface.
Initially partially molten surface regions grow and merge until the particle becomes fully molten at a higher temperature.
TEM will reveal partial melting at nanoparticle surfaces below the bulk melting temperature.
A premelting DSC endotherm will precede the main melting endotherm.
Melting will progress inward until the entire nanoparticle liquefies near the expected bulk melting temperature.
A pure metal or homogeneous alloy without significant surface segregation conventionally melts at its equilibrium melting point without an early liquid-like surface layer.
The proposed surface-premelting phenomenon should be most evident in sub-50 nm FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles under inert or vacuum conditions.
Thicker oxide layers may obscure or delay early surface melting.
Larger particle sizes may obscure or delay early surface melting.
The temperature range and layer thickness of surface melting depend on local composition, particle size, and surface contamination.
Absence of both a pre-bulk-melting surface liquid layer in TEM and an early DSC endotherm would falsify the hypothesis.
